doc.title: Anat Cohen interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 9, 2021

title: Mind during performance: the Tiny Desk concert and being in the moment
summary: She describes surrendering to the music, avoiding planning ahead, and the rare moments when everything clicks.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Beautiful. I want to ask you about two specific performances that are viewable for people, one is the “Tiny Desk” concert you did, Marcello Goncalves — is that correct?

And it’s really interesting to watch. First of all there’s no music in front of you and this one particular song, I’m not sure you opened your eyes at all. So this could be a — may not even have an answer, but can you describe what’s going on in your head in a kind of performance like that? Is some of it, okay here comes that chord that I have to remember to observe in my playing? Or is it different than that?

Wow that’s a really — it’s an interesting question because there’s no absolute answer to that. The goal is not to have those thoughts that you just described, because we spend hours and hours on our craft so once we get to the moment of truth, which means being on stage or being filmed, you can surrender a hundred percent to the music and be in the moment, and really be in tune with that bigger thing, which is the music, which is beyond what I know and what I can do and what I need — it’s what the music needs, and how to connect with the other person and how to connect with the rest of the world. And I think that’s the goal. I think if you are, and that kind of takes me to think about improvisation and playing jazz, if you are playing a song and concentrating on oh that moment is coming and I need to think about the chord — if you’re thinking about what is upcoming and making a plan you are no longer in the moment so you’re losing the moment. So of course it’s kind of incredible I think, you know and you mentioned the classical world and the classical music and the high skill it takes for a musician to execute what they need to do on their instrument, on the whole craft of playing an instrument, being an instrumentalist and being an improviser and being a connector and a communicator, it’s a lot of things and we have a lot of thoughts. In other moments I will be on stage and maybe I’ll start thinking about, wait did I shut off the gas before I left the house or did I — or you know, or somebody would walk into the club and you’re like oh wow wait, I forgot to call or they e-mailed me. Who knows? So many different thoughts can come in into while you’re playing a solo, and it’s like you know when we’re meditating and we have thoughts. And do we surrender to them and let them take over or just like okay shew — it’s a thought, concentrate, go back, distraction. But I think the goal is to get to that connection with the moment that’s really, those tiny moments where you are — it’s the safest place in the world I think when you’re inside the music sphere, when you are connected with the music, with the other musicians, everybody is like in that place and you are laser focused on the moment. And there is some kind of like, you feel the energy of the audience and you feel the energy of — everything just clicks and comes together © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

and makes sense. And sometimes it’s the most obvious thing. It makes sense. Music can be something so simple and those are like tiny, tiny moments in a whole many many hours of like confusion and frustration and battles and travels. So this is the goal is to get to those moments, to work on our craft to a point where we could master those moments and really bring them to life.
